reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Defined histologically by a marked increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes (predominantly CD8-positive T cells) within the surface and foveolar epithelium
Strongly associated with coeliac disease and with Helicobacter pylori infection, which together account for most cases
May appear endoscopically as varioliform gastritis, with nodularity, thickened folds, and aphthoid erosions typically in the gastric body
Many patients are asymptomatic or have non-specific dyspepsia, and the diagnosis is often made on biopsy performed for other reasons
Treatment is directed at the underlying cause, such as eradicating Helicobacter pylori or instituting a gluten-free diet for coeliac disease
The lymphocytosis and symptoms frequently resolve once the associated condition is treated
Rarely it is linked to protein loss producing a Menetrier-like picture or to lymphoma, warranting careful assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphocytic gastritis is a histological pattern characterised by a striking accumulation of intraepithelial T lymphocytes within the gastric surface and pit epithelium, accompanied by a chronic mononuclear infiltrate in the lamina propria. It is regarded as an immune-mediated mucosal response rather than a distinct disease, most often triggered by gluten sensitivity in coeliac disease or by Helicobacter pylori infection, both of which drive an intraepithelial lymphocytic reaction analogous to that seen in the coeliac duodenum. The inflammatory response can distort the surface epithelium and produce the nodular, erosive (varioliform) appearance seen at endoscopy.
additionalDifferentials: Menetrier disease and other hypertrophic gastropathies
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with gastric biopsies for histology and immunohistochemical quantification of intraepithelial lymphocytes
Helicobacter pylori testing by histology, urea breath test, stool antigen, or serology
Coeliac serology and duodenal biopsies to detect associated coeliac disease
Full blood count and iron studies to assess for anaemia
Serum albumin where a protein-losing, Menetrier-like picture is suspected
Repeat biopsy after treatment of the underlying cause to confirm resolution
redFlags: Marked protein loss with hypoalbuminaemia suggesting a hypertrophic, Menetrier-like variant
Persistent nodularity or a mass raising concern for lymphoma
Refractory symptoms or histology despite treating coeliac disease and Helicobacter pylori
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally good, with the lymphocytic infiltrate and symptoms typically improving after eradication of Helicobacter pylori or introduction of a gluten-free diet, although the histological pattern may persist in a minority.
pitfalls: Reporting the pattern without searching for the underlying coeliac disease or Helicobacter pylori
Missing coeliac disease by not taking duodenal biopsies or checking serology
Overlooking a rare protein-losing or lymphomatous complication
Assuming persistence of the histological pattern equates to treatment failure
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
